title: The Locked Box

beats.text: In nineteen eleven, Standard Oil got smashed into thirty-four pieces. And John D. Rockefeller got richer.
It once refined nine of every ten American barrels, and it loved secrets.
Then the Supreme Court gives it six months to split up.
Your one stock becomes thirty-four, a slice of every piece.
Rockefeller owns a quarter. Surely, this ends him.
Two years later, the pieces are worth twice the old whole.
So how does chopping something up make it bigger?
You see, picture a locked toolbox at a yard sale.
Open it, tag every tool, and the same stuff sells for more.
Standard Oil was that locked box.
The breakup made investors look inside and price every piece.
Same refineries. Same pipelines. Same oil.
The court didn't shrink Rockefeller. It opened his box.

facts.claim: US Supreme Court ruled on May 15, 1911 that Standard Oil be dissolved
Broken into 34 companies (Britannica/one wiki section say 33; ABA says 37 - narration uses 34, the majority figure)
Six months to carry out the breakup
Standard Oil controlled about 90% of American refining (1879 / late 1880s)
Standard Oil was secretive (secret subsidiaries, secret trust agreement, no full accounts of subsidiaries)
Every shareholder received a pro rata slice of shares in each of the 34 companies
Rockefeller owned about a quarter of the shares (SPE: nearly 30%)
Within about two years the pieces were worth roughly double (GFD: combined ~$665M in 1911 vs ~$1,263M in 1913; PSU: 1913 value doubled; wellwiki: share values mostly doubled)
Rockefeller's fortune tripled after the breakup (Orbis: ~$300M to ~$900M in two years)
The breakup forced investors to investigate the true value of Standard Oil and its subsidiaries; the pieces were worth more separately than as one

caption:
1911: the Supreme Court broke Standard Oil into 34 companies, and every shareholder got a slice of each.
Two years later the pieces were worth about twice the old whole, and Rockefeller's fortune had tripled. Same refineries, same oil: investors could finally price every piece.
